topics.summary: Covers isolating members, choosing axes, and understanding what roller, pin, fixed, and internal hinge supports permit and restrain in 2D plane structures.
subtopics: Isolating a structure or member from its surroundings

Pin support: 2 reaction components (Rx, Ry); permits rotation
Fixed support: 3 reaction components (Rx, Ry, Mz); restrains translation and rotation
Internal hinge (pin release): transmits shear/axial force but enforces M = 0 at the hinge
learningObjectives: Identify the exact number and direction of reaction components for any idealised support.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is true regarding the dot (scalar) product and cross (vector) product of two nonzero, nonparallel three-dimensional vectors P and Q?
assumptions: Idealized rigid-body static equilibrium with consistent SI metric units.
options: Both the dot product and the cross product are commutative: P · Q = Q · P and P × Q = Q × P.
The dot product is commutative (P · Q = Q · P), whereas the cross product is anti-commutative (P × Q = -Q × P).

questions.prompt: A coplanar couple consists of two parallel forces of equal magnitude F separated by a perpendicular distance d and acting in opposite directions. Which statement accurately describes the moment of this couple?
assumptions: Idealized rigid-body static equilibrium with consistent SI metric units.
options: The moment of the couple is zero about the midpoint between the two forces.
The moment of the couple is a free vector of magnitude Fd that is independent of the choice of moment center O.
The moment of the couple is inversely proportional to the distance from the origin O.
The couple produces both a net translational resultant force 2F and a moment Fd.
questions.explanation: Because the two forces are equal and opposite, their vector sum is zero (no net translation). Taking moments about any point O yields M = r1 × F + r2 × (-F) = (r1 - r2) × F, which has magnitude Fd and is independent of the location of point O.

questions.prompt: According to Varignon's theorem, how can the moment of a force F about a fixed point O be evaluated?
assumptions: Idealized rigid-body static equilibrium with consistent SI metric units.
options: It is equal to the dot product of the position vector r and the force vector F.
It is equal to the algebraic (or vector) sum of the moments of the components of F about the same point O.
It is equal to the magnitude of F divided by the perpendicular distance from O to the line of action.
It is zero whenever the force is resolved into rectangular components.
questions.explanation: Varignon's theorem states that the moment of a force about any point is equal to the algebraic (or vector) sum of the moments of the components of the force about that point, which follows directly from the distributive law of the cross product: r × (F1 + F2) = r × F1 + r × F2.

assumptions: Idealized rigid-body static equilibrium with consistent SI metric units.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Step 1: Taking the datum at O, for a small angular displacement theta from the vertical, the center of gravity (at L/2) drops by (L/2)(1 - cos(theta)) and the top spring stretches by L sin(theta) ≈ Ltheta. hints: First Hint (Governing Structural Principle: Evaluate determinacy of a two-span continuous beam): Isolate the structural member from its supports and replace each physical restraint with the exact force or moment reactions it can develop.

Second Hint (Analytical Elimination Criterion): Count restraint components: a roller develops 1 reaction normal to the rolling surface, a pin develops 2 orthogonal force reactions (R_x, R_y), and a fixed support develops 3 reactions (R_x, R_y, M_fixed). Eliminate distractors that violate equilibrium, confuse elastic stiffness (E·I) with yield strength (f_y), or misapply Eurocode limit-state rules (Ref: Ch. 2, §2.1–2.3 (Support Idealisation & Free-Body Diagrams)).
